question: How do Web publishers, crawler operators, and standards participants disagree about whether robots.txt grants permission, merely states preferences, or has legal significance?

claims.text: RFC 9309 frames robots.txt as rules crawlers are requested to honor, and says those rules are not a form of access authorization.
acceptable_patterns: not a form of access authorization

evidence_passages.text: RFC 9309 defines robots.txt as a protocol for crawler behavior and expressly says it is not access authorization.

"These rules are not a form of access authorization." (Section 1.3) ... "crawlers are requested to honor when accessing URIs" (Section 1.3), framing the rules as guidance rather than mandatory enforcement.

rejected_claims.text: robots.txt universally grants permission to crawl.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied RFC 9309 evidence saying robots.txt rules are not a form of access authorization.

rejected_claims.text: Standards participants agree that robots.txt is only a preference signal with no claimed legal significance.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by supplied evidence about TDM reservation protocols, the AI-Pref draft, and EDRLab notes about reservation of rights.

rejected_claims.text: robots.txt alone creates binding legal duties everywhere.
rejected_claims.reason: Overly broad and unsupported; the supplied evidence explicitly says there is not good evidence of a universal rule.

rejected_claims.text: All crawler operators describe robots.txt the same way.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by supplied evidence showing both advisory language and stronger permission language.

rejected_claims.text: Publishers uniformly treat robots.txt as legally binding.
rejected_claims.reason: Contradicted by the supplied Medium evidence calling it a voluntary technical standard and not a legally binding arrangement.

rejected_claims.text: Google documentation similarly treats robots.txt as traffic management rather than enforcement: it says robots.txt cannot enforce crawler behavior, is not by itself a way to keep pages out of Google, and disallowed URLs can still appear in search results.
rejected_claims.reason: La source Google (developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) n'a jamais été ouverte : opened_urls est vide dans l'exécution Codex et l'unique evidence_passage attaché à cette URL est une copie du final_answer, pas un extrait de la page. De plus, deux des trois acceptable_patterns (« not a way to keep pages out of Google by itself », « disallowed URLs can still appear in search results ») sont des paraphrases du modèle et non des citations vérifiées, ce qui rend le motif de notation à la fois invérifiable et trop étroit.

rejected_claims.text: Within standards work, one W3C Community Group document defines a separate TDM Reservation Protocol capable of expressing reservation of rights under EU copyright law and says it is not a W3C Standard.
rejected_claims.reason: Les citations « capable of expressing the reservation of rights » et « not a W3C Standard » ne reposent que sur l'auto-citation du final_answer Codex ; le rapport CG-FINAL-tdmrep-20240510 ne figure ni dans opened_urls ni dans un résultat d'outil exposé, et l'exécution Claude n'en dit rien. Impossible de confirmer le libellé exact ni l'attribution.

rejected_claims.text: The same W3C Community Group later said using robots.txt as a search opt-in is only a complementary solution, that this complementarity remains subject to interpretation, and that a more explicit signal could be more secure.
rejected_claims.reason: Même défaut de sourçage (w3.org/community/tdmrep/ jamais ouvert, evidence_passage = final_answer). En outre, le pattern « more explicit signal could be more secure » est une reformulation interprétative et non une citation littérale, et l'affirmation dépend d'une lecture non explicitée du texte du groupe ; motif de notation non déterministe.

rejected_claims.text: Standards participants also disagree about legal significance for AI uses: an IETF draft proposes robots.txt carry usage preferences, while EDRLab meeting notes say an AI-Pref signal in robots.txt is logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights under EU CDSM Article 4.
rejected_claims.reason: Revendication la plus risquée : elle repose sur draft-ietf-aipref-attach/05 et sur des notes EDRLab datées d'avril 2026, aucune des deux n'ayant été ouverte ni exposée par un résultat d'outil. La citation distinctive « logically sufficient to express a reservation of rights » sous l'article 4 de la directive CDSM est invérifiable et transforme une note de réunion en position juridique tranchée — surinterprétation d'une source non confirmée.

rejected_claims.text: Crawler operators use mixed language too: Google says its common crawlers always obey robots.txt rules, while OpenAI advertiser guidance says robots.txt tells crawlers whether they are permitted to access parts of a site.
rejected_claims.reason: Les deux sources (docs Google common crawlers et l'article d'aide OpenAI 20001243) ne sont ni ouvertes ni corroborées ; l'identifiant de l'article OpenAI ne peut être validé à partir de l'évidence fournie. La revendication fusionne par ailleurs deux affirmations distinctes en un seul énoncé, ce qui rend la notation lexicale ambiguë (un seul pattern satisfait suffirait à valider un contenu partiel).

rejected_claims.text: Publishers are split as well: Medium describes robots.txt as where it tells bots what they are and are not allowed to crawl, but the same post also says robots.txt is not a legally binding arrangement and is a voluntary technical standard.
rejected_claims.reason: Les citations Medium (« isn’t a legally binding arrangement », « voluntary technical standard ») ne proviennent que du final_answer Codex ; l'URL du billet apparaît dans les requêtes mais n'a jamais été ouverte, et aucun résultat d'outil n'en expose le contenu. Le pattern comportant l'apostrophe typographique « isn’t » est de surcroît fragile pour une notation lexicale déterministe.
